hints: Start by remembering what happens in transcription - the template strand is read to build a complementary RNA strand, so think which RNA base pairs with each DNA base and what replaces thymine in RNA.
walkthrough:
Pair DNA Template to RNA**
Think of the template as a mould. RNA polymerase adds complementary free RNA nucleotides: C pairs with G, G pairs with C, A pairs with U, and T pairs with A. Remember RNA has uracil (U) instead of thymine.

Read Across Positions 1-12**
Applying that rule to C-A-C-T-A-C-T-C-C-A-A-C gives G-U-G-A-U-G-A-G-G-U-U-G. That is your primary transcript (pre-mRNA) sequence.
Final answer: Primary transcript (positions 1-12): G U G A U G A G G U U G

hints: Look at Table 4.2 and split the DNA template in Table 4.1 into groups of three starting at position 1 - which triplet do you get for aa1, aa2, aa3 and aa4, and where does each appear in Table 4.2?
walkthrough:
Split Into Triplets**
Codons are read in threes. From the template: positions 1-3 = CAC, 4-6 = TAC, 7-9 = TCC, 10-12 = AAC.

Match to Table 4.2**
CAC is listed under val, TAC is the only triplet for met, TCC is listed under arg, AAC is listed under leu. So the sequence is val-met-arg-leu.
Final answer: aa1 = val (valine); aa2 = met (methionine); aa3 = arg (arginine); aa4 = leu (leucine)

hints: Focus on the first triplet CAC for aa1 and check Table 4.2 - how many different triplets all give the same amino acid as CAC?
Think about what the word degenerate means for the genetic code - if the changed triplet still codes for the same amino acid, what happens to protein structure?
walkthrough:
What Changes at Position 3?**
Position 3 is the third base of the aa1 triplet CAC. A substitution changes CAC to CAA, CAG or CAT depending on the new base.

Why No Effect on Protein**
Table 4.2 shows CAA, CAG, CAT and CAC all code for valine. Because the code is degenerate, more than one triplet codes for the same amino acid. So aa1 is still valine, the primary structure is unchanged, and the final 3D protein is unchanged. This is a silent mutation.
Final answer: No effect on protein structure. All four triplets beginning with CA (CAA, CAG, CAT, CAC) code for valine, as the genetic code is degenerate / redundant.

hints: Compare removing one base with swapping one base - if you delete position 3, what happens to the total number of bases and how the rest are grouped into threes?
Think about what happens to every triplet after the deletion point - will aa2, aa3 and aa4 stay the same?
Consider the knock-on effects on protein shape - if the amino acid sequence changes, what could happen to folding, and what if a stop codon appears early?
walkthrough:
Why Deletion Is Different**
Substitution keeps the reading frame. Deletion of position 3 removes one nucleotide, so every base after it moves one place left. The triplets are now regrouped differently.

Frameshift Effect**
The first triplet can still be read as val, but from the mutation onwards all codons change. That means aa2, aa3, aa4 and beyond will be different amino acids, so the primary structure is altered.

Consequence for Final Protein**
A different sequence of amino acids folds differently, so tertiary structure, e.g. active site or binding site shape, changes and function is usually lost. The new frame may also bring in a stop codon early, terminating translation prematurely to give a shorter, non-functional polypeptide.

Final answer: Frameshift mutation with major effect. First amino acid still val; all codons downstream shift, altering all subsequent amino acids / primary structure, altering tertiary structure; may create premature stop codon giving shorter polypeptide.

hints: Remember when DNA amount doubles before mitosis - which large phase includes G1, S and G2, and which S sub-phase has S for synthesis?
walkthrough:
Where DNA Doubles**
Nuclear DNA is replicated once per cycle during interphase, specifically in S phase (synthesis phase) between G1 and G2, before mitosis and cytokinesis.

Which Circles**
So you circle both interphase (the whole preparation period) and S phase (the exact part where replication occurs).
Final answer: Circle interphase and S phase.

hints: Start with how the two strands are separated - which enzyme breaks which bonds to unwind the helix?
Think about what each exposed strand is used for and what raw materials are added to build the new strand.
Recall the main building enzyme that joins new nucleotides and how the two new strands differ in continuous versus fragmented synthesis.
Finish by explaining how fragments are joined and why the result is called semi-conservative.
walkthrough:
Unwinding the Helix**
Helicase unwinds the double helix and breaks hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, exposing both strands so each can act as a template.

Adding New Nucleotides**
Free activated DNA nucleotides pair complementarily with exposed bases. DNA polymerase adds them and catalyses formation of phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, with proofreading for mismatches.

Leading and Lagging Strands**
One new strand (leading strand) is synthesised continuously towards the replication fork. The other (lagging strand) is synthesised away from the fork in short Okazaki fragments.

Joining and Result**
DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments with phosphodiester bonds. Each of the two resulting double helices contains one original parental strand and one newly synthesised strand, so replication is semi-conservative.

Final answer: Helicase unwinds helix breaking hydrogen bonds; both strands act as templates; free activated DNA nucleotides added complementarily by DNA polymerase forming phosphodiester bonds; leading strand continuous, lagging strand as Okazaki fragments joined by ligase; semi-conservative - each new DNA has one parental and one new strand.

hints: Look at bracket A in Fig. 4.1 - it points to the five-carbon sugar in the middle of ATP, so recall which pentose is found in RNA and ATP versus DNA.
walkthrough:
Identify Part A**
ATP is adenine + pentose sugar + three phosphates. Bracket A shows the five-carbon sugar with two OH groups.

Name the Sugar**
That sugar is ribose (not deoxyribose as in DNA). So A is ribose.
